speaker: Patient
text: 50-year-old male. The patient reports a progressively increasing swelling on the nape of his neck for 2 months. He denies having a fever, pain, or any discharge from the swelling. He mentions a history of colon cancer for which he underwent colectomy at the age of 43. He also has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and osteoarthritis of the left knee. He takes insulin glargine, metformin, enalapril, and naproxen.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your history of colon cancer, I need to rule out metastasis, so could you describe if the swelling feels soft and doughy or hard and fixed to the underlying tissue? REQUEST TEST: Ultrasound of the neck mass.

speaker: Doctor
text: The ultrasound suggests a benign cystic lesion, likely a lipoma or sebaceous cyst, but given your history, we must be thorough. Does the mass feel mobile under the skin, or is it fixed to deeper structures? REQUEST TEST: Fine Needle Aspiration of the neck mass.

speaker: Doctor
text: The normal FNA is surprising for a cystic lesion, so I need to clarify the texture further. Does the mass feel fluctuant like a water balloon, or is it firm and rubbery? REQUEST TEST: MRI of the neck.

speaker: Doctor
text: The normal FNA and MRI results are puzzling for a visible subcutaneous mass, so I need to rule out a lipoma or other benign soft tissue tumor that might not show up as clearly on these specific scans. Does the mass feel soft and doughy, consistent with a lipoma, or is it firm and rubbery? REQUEST TEST: CT scan of the neck.

speaker: Doctor
text: This is highly unusual for a visible mass to be completely normal on US, MRI, and CT, so I need to clarify if the swelling is truly subcutaneous or if it might be related to the underlying bone or muscle. Does the swelling increase in size when you stand up or strain, suggesting a herniation or vascular issue? REQUEST TEST: Biopsy of the neck mass.

speaker: Doctor
text: This is extremely unusual, as a visible mass should not have normal imaging and biopsy results. Can you clarify if the swelling is actually in the subcutaneous tissue or if it might be related to the underlying bone or muscle structure? REQUEST IMAGES

speaker: Doctor
text: The images show a classic "dimpling" sign when the skin is pinched, which is diagnostic for a lipoma. DIAGNOSIS READY: Lipoma
